title: Your Largest Customer Just Left
companyContext: A car-parts manufacturer you've held for a long time. Its single largest customer just cancelled a big supply contract.

stages.headline: "Company's largest customer, representing 40% of revenue, cancels multi-year supply contract, citing a shift to a competing supplier"
stages.note: This customer relationship has been the company's single biggest revenue source for years.

fundamentals.Cash reserves: Cover ~5 months of operating expenses at current burn rate

stages.note: Revenue at risk of ~40% of last year's total means nearly half its income just walked out the door. Cash reserves covering ~5 months of running costs means a limited cushion. No confirmed replacement customers means this is what's known today - no replacement deal has been confirmed.
Fallen sharply since the cancellation was announced.

choices.label: Buy more
choices.description: The market may be overreacting, add.

criteria.description: Recognizes that 40% of revenue is at risk from a single customer loss - a major, concentrated impact, not a minor one.
Notes that no replacement contract has been confirmed and weighs the limited cash runway against that gap.
Treats this as a genuine fundamental deterioration to respond to, rather than a sentiment-driven overreaction to simply wait out.

factorOptions.label: 40% of last year's revenue is now at risk from a single customer loss

rubric.idealSummary: Losing a customer worth 40% of revenue, with no replacement confirmed and only a few months of cash, is a real change to the business - not a market mood swing. This is exactly the kind of concrete, measurable news a disciplined exit is supposed to respond to. Whether you sell is judged by what you knew when you decided - not by whatever the price happens to do afterward.

outcome.summary: Six weeks later, with no advance signal, the company announced a surprise replacement contract with an even bigger customer. The stock recovered and rallied past its old level. Someone who sold took a real loss and missed the rebound - and their decision was still sound. Nothing available at the time hinted at a rescue, and a 40%-of-revenue loss with no backup was a legitimate reason to cut risk. Good decisions are judged by the information you had, not by how the story ends.

survivorshipNote: A deliberately included 'sound decision, unlucky outcome' case - the stock's own price history recovers strongly after a legitimately sound exit. This is precisely the scenario that shows why grading on outcome instead of process would have punished the right decision.
